Glamorgan
gluh-MOR-gun
n. (the southern Welsh county of the Vale and the coalfield, seat of the see of Llandaff and the ground of the first Welsh field preaching)
Welsh Gwlad Morgan, the land of Morgan, from a tenth-century ruler of the district; anglicised as Glamorgan.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Glamorgan is the southern Welsh county, holding the fertile Vale along the coast, the uplands behind it and the valleys that were later cut open for iron and coal. The see of Llandaff stands in it, and so do the old Cistercian houses of Margam and Neath, dissolved with the rest in the sixteen-thirties of the previous century's reckoning; the county's gentry took the abbey lands and with them a settled interest in the Reformation. Its importance to the dictionary is that Glamorgan is where Welsh field preaching began in earnest. Howell Harris of Trevecca, converted in 1735, carried his exhorting west and south; Daniel Rowland came over from Cardiganshire; and the Calvinistic Methodist societies multiplied through the Vale and the hill parishes faster than any parish church could hold them. When the ironworks at Merthyr and Dowlais and then the coal of the Rhondda drew tens of thousands into the valleys, the chapels went with them, and the industrial population of south Wales was evangelised as it was gathered. The harvest figure is the right one for the county and the labourers were few. The dictionary records Glamorgan as a place where the Word went out to men at their work, and where the going out was done by preachers the establishment had not sent.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a vale as a tract of low ground between hills; a mine as a pit from which minerals are taken; harvest as the season of gathering; a labourer as one who works; and to itinerate as to travel from place to place.

expand to see more

VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.

MINE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, from which metals, coal and other mineral substances are taken.

HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn gathered.

LABOURER, n. One who labours in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill.

ITINERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.

Key Scripture

Deu 8:9 — "A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass."

Mat 9:37 — "Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;"

Act 8:4 — "Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word."

Ecc 5:9 — "Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field."

Modern Corruption

Southern Welsh county of the Vale, the see of Llandaff and the coalfield, where Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland began the field preaching that gathered the industrial valleys the parish system could not hold.

expand to see more

The corruption the county invites is the identifying of plenty with blessing. Glamorgan was a land whose stones were iron, and the promise of Deuteronomy sounds almost like a description of it, “a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass” (Deu 8:9); but the promise is attached to a covenant and followed in that chapter by the warning not to forget the God who gave it. The valleys produced wealth and they consumed men, and the chapels that were built over the pitheads were built in the knowledge that “the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9) and that the men who raise the profit are not therefore served themselves.

The second word is against the parish order of the eighteenth century, and the dictionary speaks it plainly because the order was its own. A settled ministry that would not go to where the people had moved left the harvest standing, and the exhorters who went were irregular men without orders or licence. Our Lord's own account of the case is that “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and the apostolic precedent for preaching done by the unordained scattered is express, for “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). An establishment that answers such preaching with prosecution has mistaken the disorder for the disease.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek therismos (G2326), harvest; Greek ergates (G2040), a labourer; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad.

expand to see more

Greek therismos (G2326) — the harvest, the act or the crop; “The harvest truly is plenteous”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; “but the labourers are few”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad as seed; “they that were scattered abroad”, Acts 8:4.

Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to announce good news, to preach the gospel; “went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.

Hebrew sadeh (H7704) — a field, open country; “the king himself is served by the field”, Ecclesiastes 5:9.

Usage

"“a land whose stones are iron” (Deu 8:9) — the ironworks of Merthyr and Dowlais."

"“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — the valleys outgrowing the parishes."

"“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — Harris and Rowland without licence."
